subject: biology
title: Adaptive immunity
summary: Explains the third line of defence: antigen presentation, clonal selection, the humoral response with B cells and antibodies, the cell-mediated response with T cells, and primary versus secondary responses.
body:
Once you have had chickenpox, you almost never catch it again. That lasting protection comes from the **adaptive immune response**, the third line of defence. It is slower to start than the innate response, but it is highly specific to each antigen and it remembers pathogens it has met before. This is also the system that vaccines rely on.

## Think of it like this

### Clonal selection is like a footy club's huge list of squad players

Imagine a footy club with millions of players on its list, each trained for exactly one opposition team. Before any game is fixtured, the whole list already exists, just as the body already holds millions of **lymphocytes**, each with one receptor shape. When a particular opponent (an **antigen**) turns up, the coach doesn't train a new player; he picks the one player who matches (**clonal selection**). That player is then copied many times over (**clonal expansion**) until there is a full team of identical specialists, some playing today (**effector cells**) and some kept on the bench for next season (**memory cells**).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* real lymphocytes copy themselves by mitosis into genetically identical cells, and most of the cells on the "list" are never picked at all, so many die without ever being used.

### Helper T cells are like a team captain calling the plays

A **dendritic cell** is like a scout who grabs a bit of the opposition's game footage, takes it back to the clubrooms (the **lymph node**) and shows it on a screen (**MHC class II**). Only the **helper T cell** whose receptor fits that footage reacts. It then shouts instructions (**cytokines**) that switch on both the B cell "defenders" and the cytotoxic T cell "tacklers". Take the captain off the field, as HIV does, and the whole team plays badly, which is why losing helper T cells weakens both the **humoral** and **cell-mediated** responses.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a captain makes choices, but helper T cells don't "decide" anything; they are activated chemically when their receptor binds a complementary antigen on MHC II.

### The humoral and cell-mediated responses are like security at a music festival

Security guards in the crowd deal with troublemakers who are out in the open: they tag them with wristbands so others can spot and remove them. That is like **antibodies** from **plasma cells** binding pathogens in blood and tissue fluid, then **neutralising**, clumping (**agglutination**) and marking them (**opsonisation**) so phagocytes can deal with them. But if a troublemaker has already hidden inside a food truck, guards in the crowd can't reach them, so a separate team shuts that truck down. That is the **cytotoxic T cell** recognising an infected cell by its **MHC class I** display and using **perforin** and **granzymes** to trigger **apoptosis**.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the infected cell isn't a hiding place that gets emptied; the cell itself is destroyed in a controlled way, along with the virus being made inside it.

### In real life

This is why you usually only get chickenpox once, and why booster shots are given: each dose builds up more **memory cells**, so a later exposure triggers a **secondary response** that is faster, bigger and longer-lasting. It is also why people with untreated HIV become vulnerable to infections that a healthy immune system would easily control.

## Key ideas

### Features of the third line of defence

The adaptive response is:

- **specific**: each lymphocyte recognises one particular antigen;
- **slower at first**: a first response takes days to build up;
- **with memory**: a second exposure to the same antigen produces a faster, stronger response.

The cells of the adaptive response are **lymphocytes**: **B cells** and **T cells**. Both form in the bone marrow. B cells mature in the bone marrow; T cells mature in the thymus. During maturation, lymphocytes that react strongly to self antigens are removed, which helps prevent attacks on the body's own tissues.

Each lymphocyte has thousands of identical receptors on its surface that fit one antigen shape. The specific part of an antigen that a receptor binds to is called an **epitope** (or antigenic determinant). Because receptor genes are rearranged randomly as lymphocytes develop, the body contains millions of different lymphocytes, each with a different receptor, before it ever meets a pathogen.

### Antigen presentation

T cells cannot recognise free antigen. They only recognise antigen fragments displayed on MHC markers. **Antigen presentation** is the display of these fragments.

1. An antigen-presenting cell (APC), usually a **dendritic cell**, engulfs a pathogen in the tissues by phagocytosis.
2. It breaks the pathogen into fragments and loads them onto **MHC class II** markers on its surface.
3. It travels through lymph vessels to a lymph node.
4. In the lymph node, the APC presents the antigen to **helper T cells**. Only the helper T cell whose receptor fits that MHC II and antigen combination binds.

Infected body cells display fragments of the pathogen's proteins on **MHC class I**, which is how cytotoxic T cells recognise them.

### Clonal selection and clonal expansion

**Clonal selection** is the process in which only the lymphocyte whose receptor matches the antigen is selected and activated. It then undergoes **clonal expansion**: it divides rapidly by mitosis to make a large population of identical cells (a **clone**) with the same receptor. The clone **differentiates** into effector cells that fight the infection now and memory cells that remain for the future.

This explains the delay in a first response: there are only a few matching lymphocytes at the start, and it takes days to find, activate and multiply them.

### Helper T cells: the coordinators

**Helper T cells** (also called CD4⁺ T cells) bind to antigen on MHC II. Once activated they multiply and release **cytokines** (also called interleukins) that:

- activate B cells with the matching receptor (needed for most B cell responses);
- activate cytotoxic T cells;
- stimulate macrophages to destroy pathogens more effectively.

Because they activate both branches, losing helper T cells weakens the whole adaptive response. HIV infects and destroys helper T cells, which is why untreated HIV leads to AIDS.

### The humoral response

The **humoral response** is the antibody-based response. It targets pathogens and toxins that are outside cells, in the blood and tissue fluid ("humour" is an old word for body fluids).

1. A **naive B cell** (one not yet activated) binds an antigen that fits its receptor. It engulfs the antigen and presents fragments on MHC II.
2. A helper T cell with a matching receptor binds the B cell and releases cytokines.
3. The B cell is activated and undergoes clonal expansion.
4. The clone differentiates into **plasma cells** and **memory B cells**.

**Plasma cells** are effector cells that secrete large amounts of antibody. They have lots of rough endoplasmic reticulum to make this protein. They live only days to weeks. **Memory B cells** are long-lived and remain in the body, ready to respond quickly if the same antigen returns.

### Antibody structure

An **antibody** (or immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein made of four polypeptide chains: two identical **heavy chains** and two identical **light chains**, held together by disulfide bonds.

- The tips of the two arms are the **variable regions**. Their amino acid sequence differs between antibodies, giving each **antigen-binding site** a shape complementary to one epitope. Each antibody has two identical binding sites.
- The rest is the **constant region**, which is the same within a class of antibody. It determines how the antibody interacts with other parts of the immune system, for example binding to phagocytes or activating complement.
- A flexible **hinge region** lets the arms move so they can bind antigens at different distances apart.

### Antibody functions

Antibodies do not destroy pathogens on their own. They mark and disable them:

- **Neutralisation**: antibodies cover the parts of a virus or toxin that it uses to attach to cells, so it cannot enter or harm them.
- **Agglutination**: because each antibody has two binding sites, it can link pathogens together into clumps, which are easier for phagocytes to engulf and cannot spread as easily.
- **Opsonisation**: antibodies coat the pathogen and phagocytes bind to their constant regions, speeding up phagocytosis.
- **Complement activation**: antibodies bound to a pathogen can trigger complement, leading to lysis.

### The cell-mediated response

The **cell-mediated response** targets cells that are already infected (for example by a virus) and abnormal cells such as cancer cells. Antibodies cannot reach pathogens hidden inside cells.

1. A **cytotoxic T cell** (CD8⁺ T cell) with a matching receptor binds to antigen on MHC I on an APC.
2. With cytokines from helper T cells, it undergoes clonal expansion and differentiates into effector cytotoxic T cells and **memory T cells**.
3. Effector cytotoxic T cells travel to the infection and bind to infected body cells displaying the same antigen on **MHC I**.
4. They release **perforin** (which makes pores in the target membrane) and **granzymes** (which trigger **apoptosis**). The infected cell dies in a controlled way, so the virus cannot finish replicating.

| | Humoral response | Cell-mediated response |
|---|---|---|
| Main cells | B cells, plasma cells | Cytotoxic T cells |
| Target | Pathogens and toxins outside cells | Infected and abnormal body cells |
| How it acts | Antibodies | Direct killing by apoptosis |
| Memory cells | Memory B cells | Memory T cells |

Helper T cells are needed for both.

### Primary and secondary responses

The **primary response** happens on first exposure to an antigen. There is a lag of several days while clonal selection and expansion occur, and the antibody level rises slowly to a modest peak before falling.

The **secondary response** happens on a later exposure to the same antigen. Memory cells are already present in large numbers, so:

- the lag is much shorter;
- antibody levels rise faster;
- the peak is much higher;
- antibodies remain high for longer.

On a graph of antibody concentration (y-axis) against time (x-axis), the secondary curve is steeper, taller and starts sooner after exposure. The pathogen is usually removed before symptoms appear, so the person is **immune**.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Reading primary and secondary response data

A rabbit was injected with antigen X on day 0 and again on day 40. On day 40 it was also injected with a new antigen Y for the first time. Antibody levels were measured.

1. Anti-X after day 0: low and slow, peaking around day 10–14. This is a primary response.
2. Anti-X after day 40: rises within a couple of days to a much higher peak. This is a secondary response, due to memory B cells made after the first injection.
3. Anti-Y after day 40: low and slow, like the first anti-X curve. This is a primary response, because no memory cells for Y existed.
4. Conclusion: memory is specific. Memory cells for X do not help against Y.

### Example 2: Why a virus needs both branches

A person is infected with a respiratory virus.

1. Virus particles in fluid between cells are neutralised by antibodies (humoral) so they cannot infect new cells.
2. Cells that are already infected display viral fragments on MHC I.
3. Cytotoxic T cells recognise them and trigger apoptosis (cell-mediated), stopping new virus being made.
4. Conclusion: the humoral response stops spread; the cell-mediated response removes infected cells. Both depend on helper T cells.

### Example 3: Losing helper T cells

A patient's helper T cell count has fallen very low.

1. Without helper T cell cytokines, most B cells cannot be activated, so fewer plasma cells and antibodies are made.
2. Cytotoxic T cells are also poorly activated.
3. Conclusion: both humoral and cell-mediated immunity fail, so the patient becomes vulnerable to many infections.

## Common mistakes

- Saying B cells make antibodies directly. Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells, which differentiate from activated B cells.
- Thinking antibodies kill pathogens themselves. They neutralise, agglutinate and mark pathogens; phagocytes and complement do the destroying.
- Mixing up MHC classes: helper T cells read MHC II; cytotoxic T cells recognise infected cells by MHC I.
- Writing that the antigen creates matching lymphocytes. The matching lymphocyte already exists; the antigen selects it.
- Describing the secondary response as only "faster". Full marks usually need faster, greater and longer-lasting, with the reason (memory cells).

## Exam tips

- Learn the humoral and cell-mediated sequences in order, naming each cell and what it does. Extended-response questions often ask for a whole sequence.
- Be ready to label an antibody diagram: heavy and light chains, variable region, antigen-binding site, constant region, hinge.
- On response graphs, describe the shape (lag time, rate, peak height, duration) and explain each difference using memory cells.
- Use "complementary" to describe how an antigen-binding site fits an epitope, not "the same shape".

## Tips to remember

- **The "rule of 8" for MHC:** multiply the CD number by the MHC class and you always get 8. Helper T cells are CD4⁺ and read **MHC II** (4 × 2 = 8); cytotoxic T cells are CD8⁺ and read **MHC I** (8 × 1 = 8).
- **"B for Bone marrow, T for Thymus":** both form in the bone marrow, but B cells mature in the **B**one marrow and T cells mature in the **T**hymus.
- **Picture a lock-and-key shop, not a key-cutting shop:** millions of lymphocytes, each with a different receptor, already exist. The antigen does not make a new key; it **selects** the lymphocyte that already fits (clonal selection), which then copies itself by mitosis (clonal expansion).
- **Antibodies "NAOC" on the door, they don't break it down** (made-up trick): **N**eutralisation, **A**gglutination, **O**psonisation, **C**omplement activation. Antibodies mark and disable; phagocytes and complement do the destroying.
- **Humoral = fluids, cell-mediated = inside cells:** antibodies from plasma cells handle pathogens floating in blood and tissue fluid; cytotoxic T cells use perforin and granzymes to trigger apoptosis in cells where the pathogen is hiding. Helper T cells are the coach for both teams.
- **Quick self-check on the secondary response:** can you say "**faster, bigger, longer**" and then "because memory cells are already there in large numbers"? If you only said "faster", you've left marks behind.

## Key terms

- **Adaptive immune response** — specific defence that develops memory.
- **Epitope** — the part of an antigen that a receptor or antibody binds to.
- **Antigen presentation** — display of antigen fragments on MHC markers.
- **Clonal selection** — activation of only the lymphocyte whose receptor matches the antigen.
- **Clonal expansion** — rapid mitosis of a selected lymphocyte to form a clone.
- **Helper T cell** — T cell that reads antigen on MHC II and releases cytokines to activate other cells.
- **Cytotoxic T cell** — T cell that kills infected or abnormal cells displaying antigen on MHC I.
- **Plasma cell** — effector B cell that secretes antibodies.
- **Memory cell** — long-lived lymphocyte that allows a faster, stronger response on re-exposure.
- **Antibody** — Y-shaped protein with variable antigen-binding sites that binds a specific antigen.
- **Humoral response** — antibody-based response against extracellular pathogens and toxins.
- **Cell-mediated response** — T cell response against infected and abnormal body cells.

## Summary

- Adaptive immunity is specific, slower at first and has memory; it uses B and T lymphocytes.
- APCs present antigen on MHC II to helper T cells, which activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
- Clonal selection activates the matching lymphocyte, which expands into effector and memory cells.
- In the humoral response, plasma cells secrete antibodies that neutralise, agglutinate and opsonise pathogens and activate complement.
- In the cell-mediated response, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells displaying antigen on MHC I by apoptosis.
- The secondary response is faster, larger and longer-lasting than the primary response because of memory cells.

questions.explanation: Plasma cells are the effector cells formed from activated B cells, and they secrete antibodies. Memory B cells are tempting because they are also B-cell derived, but they do not secrete antibodies until they are reactivated and form new plasma cells.

questions.prompt: The region of an antibody that gives it specificity for one epitope is the

options.A: variable region at the tips of the arms.
options.B: constant region of the heavy chains.

questions.explanation: The variable regions differ in amino acid sequence, forming antigen-binding sites complementary to one epitope. The constant region is tempting, but it is the same within a class and controls interaction with other immune components, not specificity.

questions.prompt: Why is there a lag of several days before antibody levels rise in a primary response?

options.A: Antibodies must first be transported from the thymus to the blood.
options.B: Only a few lymphocytes match the antigen, and time is needed for clonal selection, expansion and differentiation.
options.C: B cells must first change their receptors to fit the new antigen.
options.D: The innate response blocks the adaptive response until it has finished.

questions.explanation: Very few lymphocytes initially carry the matching receptor, so they must be selected and multiplied before enough plasma cells exist. Option C is a common misconception; the antigen selects an existing lymphocyte rather than causing the receptor to change.

questions.prompt: Antibodies are least able to act against which of the following?
questions.explanation: Antibodies cannot enter cells, so a virus replicating inside a cell is hidden from them; the cell-mediated response deals with infected cells. Option D is tempting but free virus particles between cells are exactly what neutralising antibodies target.

options.A: each antibody has two antigen-binding sites, so it can link two pathogens together.
options.B: antibodies form pores in pathogen membranes.
options.D: antibodies bind to MHC class I markers.

questions.explanation: With two binding sites, one antibody can attach to two pathogens, cross-linking many into clumps. Option B describes the membrane attack complex of complement, which antibodies can activate but do not form themselves.

questions.prompt: A mouse is given antigen P on day 0. On day 30 it is given antigen P and antigen Q. Which result is expected for the response after day 30?

options.A: Anti-P and anti-Q responses are both rapid and large.
options.B: Anti-P and anti-Q responses are both slow and small.
options.C: The anti-Q response is rapid and large; the anti-P response is slow and small.
options.D: The anti-P response is rapid and large; the anti-Q response is slow and small.

questions.explanation: Memory cells exist for P, so its response is secondary; Q is new, so its response is primary. Option A is tempting if you think the immune system is generally boosted, but memory is specific to the antigen first encountered.

questions.prompt: A virus-infected liver cell is destroyed by a cytotoxic T cell. Which statement correctly describes this event?

options.A: The cytotoxic T cell recognised viral antigen on MHC class II and engulfed the cell.
options.B: The cytotoxic T cell recognised viral antigen on MHC class I and triggered apoptosis using perforin and granzymes.
options.C: The cytotoxic T cell secreted antibodies that caused the cell to burst.
options.D: The cytotoxic T cell released histamine, which killed the cell.

questions.explanation: Liver cells are nucleated and display internal protein fragments on MHC I; cytotoxic T cells bind and induce apoptosis. Option A is wrong because ordinary body cells lack MHC II and cytotoxic T cells do not engulf their targets.

questions.prompt: A drug blocks the release of cytokines from helper T cells. Which outcome is most likely?

options.A: Only the cell-mediated response is reduced.
options.B: Only the humoral response is reduced.
options.C: Both humoral and cell-mediated responses are reduced.
options.D: Neither response is affected, because B cells and cytotoxic T cells act independently.

questions.explanation: Helper T cell cytokines are needed to activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so both branches weaken. Option B is tempting because helper T cells are often taught alongside B cells, but they activate cytotoxic T cells too.
